items.value: Assumptions 2 and 4 are valid - price incentives trigger farm investment, and higher global prices drove the poverty reduction
items.reasoning: Assumption 2 is stated almost directly: the relative price scenario shifted more than 50 per cent in favour of agriculture and 'this boosted private investments in agriculture by more than 50%'. Assumption 4 is the premise the passage's whole causal chain rests on - the price shift came 'in the wake of rising global prices', and that chain ends in 'unprecedented fall in poverty'. Assumption 1 fails on the word 'impossible'; the passage reports that India has mostly small and marginal farms and slow transformation without claiming one makes the other impossible. Assumption 3 has no basis at all - value chains, livestock and horticulture are never mentioned. Marked MED because 'essential' in assumption 4 is stronger than the passage's own wording, but it is the only remaining companion to 2 once the unmentioned assumption 3 is ruled out.

items.value: Inclusive agricultural growth is key to reducing poverty in the near future
items.reasoning: The passage asks what India did during 2005-2012 and answers entirely in agricultural terms - better relative prices, a surge in private farm investment, agri-GDP growth of 4.1 per cent, and real farm wages rising 7 per cent a year - all leading to an unprecedented fall in poverty. With half the workforce in agriculture and 85 per cent of farms small and marginal, growth that reaches those farmers and farm labourers is the demonstrated route, which is D. A picks up the China and Vietnam contrast, but the passage uses that only to diagnose India's slow transformation and never prescribes off-farm employment. B introduces farmer producer companies, which are absent from the text, and C turns an observed rise in private investment into a policy ranking against public investment that the passage never makes.

items.value: Both statements together are sufficient, neither alone is
items.reasoning: S1 tells us R beats P and Q but says nothing about S, which could still be the largest, so S1 alone is not enough. S2 only excludes S and leaves P, Q and R untested against each other, so S2 alone is not enough. Put together, S is excluded by S2 while P and Q are both below R by S1, leaving R as the largest. So the pair is sufficient and neither statement alone is.

items.value: Even together the statements do not fix n
items.reasoning: Between 10 and 20 the primes are 11, 13, 17 and 19, so S1 alone leaves four candidates. The numbers leaving remainder 1 on division by 4 are 13 and 17, so S2 alone leaves two. Taking both conditions together still leaves 13 and 17, both prime and both of the form 4k+1, so n is not determined. The answer is unchanged whether 'between 10 and 20' is read as excluding or including the endpoints.

items.value: Both statements together are sufficient, neither alone is
items.reasoning: A product of 21 alone admits 1 and 21, 3 and 7, the two negative pairs and any number of fractional pairs, so S1 alone fails. A sum of 10 alone admits infinitely many pairs, so S2 alone fails. Together they make the two numbers the roots of t squared minus 10t plus 21 = 0, which factorises as (t-3)(t-7), giving the unique pair 3 and 7. So the two statements together are sufficient.

items.value: North-West
items.reasoning: The house faces East, so its backside faces West and the first 25 metres are walked westward. Turning right while facing West points him North, so the 50 metres take him north. Turning left while facing North points him West again, so the last 25 metres take him further west. Starting from the origin he ends 50 metres west and 50 metres north of his starting point, which is the North-West direction.

items.value: Only Conclusion-I follows
items.reasoning: If every number is divisible by 2 and every number is also divisible by 3, then every number carries both factors and is therefore divisible by their least common multiple, 6 - so Conclusion-I follows. Divisibility by 4 needs a second factor of 2, which neither statement supplies; a number divisible by 2 and by 3 can be 6 or 18, neither of which is divisible by 4. So Conclusion-II does not follow.

items.value: Neither conclusion follows
items.reasoning: The statements constrain only the cats: every cat is a dog and every cat is black. Dogs that are not cats are left entirely unconstrained, so they may all be black or some may not be. Conclusion-I therefore does not follow, because non-cat dogs need not be black; and Conclusion-II does not follow either, because it is equally possible that every dog happens to be black. Since the two conclusions are contradictories and neither is forced by the premises, the answer is that neither follows.

Scanning the 26-term sequence for a position where an odd number is immediately followed by another odd number gives exactly six: 5 followed by 1, 7 followed by 3, 3 followed by 9, 5 followed by 7, 3 followed by 1, and 1 followed by 5. Note that the run 7, 3, 9 supplies two such pairs (7-3 and 3-9) and the run 3, 1, 5 likewise supplies two, which is where a hurried count typically goes wrong.

items.value: 41 boys
items.reasoning: A stands 16th from the left and G is 11 places to his right, so G is 27th from the left. V stands 18th from the right and G is 3 places further right, so G is 15th from the right. The total is therefore 27 + 15 - 1 = 41. The count is the same under the inclusive reading of 'nth from', which puts G 26th from the left and 16th from the right and again gives 41, so the two positions of G are consistent and the data are sufficient - D is wrong.

items.value: S1 and S3 together are sufficient
items.reasoning: S1 gives D above C and C above both A and B, which narrows the youngest to A or B but cannot separate them, so S1 alone fails. Adding S2 changes nothing, since S1 already implies D is the oldest, so S1 and S2 together still leave A against B - B is wrong. S2 with S3 gives D oldest and A above B but leaves C's position free, so C could be the youngest instead of B - C is wrong. S1 with S3 gives D above C above A above B, identifying B as the youngest.

The numbers from 1 to 100 containing the digit 4 are 4, 14, 24, 34, the ten numbers 40 to 49, and 54, 64, 74, 84, 94 - nineteen in all. Of these, seven are divisible by 4 (4, 24, 40, 44, 48, 64 and 84), leaving twelve that are not: 14, 34, 41, 42, 43, 45, 46, 47, 49, 54, 74 and 94. The count is 12 whether the endpoints 1 and 100 are included or excluded, since neither contains a 4.

items.value: u = 4v
items.reasoning: Doubling the side of a cube multiplies its volume by 2 cubed, so y = 8x, while the mass only doubles, so n = 2m. The two quantities are densities: u = m/x and v = n/y = 2m/8x = m/4x = u/4. Rearranging gives u = 4v. The trap is to double the volume along with the side and conclude the densities are equal.

items.value: The teacher is 35 years old
items.reasoning: Four people averaging 20 years have a combined age of 80. Writing the teacher's age as t and each student's as s gives t + 3s = 80 with |t - s| = 20. Taking the teacher as the elder, t = s + 20 gives 4s + 20 = 80, so s = 15 and t = 35. The algebraic alternative s = t + 20 yields t = 5, a five-year-old teacher of 25-year-old students, which is not among the options and is absurd in context.

A 20 per cent loss means the selling price is 80 per cent of the cost price. So cost price = 3,00,000 divided by 0.8 = 3,75,000. Checking: 20 per cent of 3,75,000 is 75,000, and 3,75,000 minus 75,000 is exactly the 3,00,000 realised. Option A, 3,60,000, comes from the common error of adding 20 per cent to the selling price instead of dividing by 0.8.

items.value: Relying on a homogeneous food source is not desirable
items.reasoning: The passage's causal core is that the Irish became 'almost wholly dependent on the potato as their staple food' while 'planting primarily one prodigious variety' whose 'genetic frailty' the fungus then exposed, killing or displacing millions. Both layers of the disaster - one crop, and one variety of it - are about homogeneity, which is D. A is wrong because the potato in fact suited Irish soil and climate very well; that is why dependence grew. B is contradicted, since the potato did become the staple. C treats the fungus as the lesson, but the passage attributes the scale of the famine to the monoculture the fungus met.

items.value: Implications 2, 3, 4 and 5 - delayed marriage and first pregnancy, early breastfeeding, safe water and sanitation, and vaccination
items.reasoning: The passage is about child undernutrition, under-five deaths and stunting, so the practical implications are the measures that act on a child's nutritional status in its earliest years - maternal age at first pregnancy, early breastfeeding, clean water and sanitation to stop nutrient loss through repeated infection, and immunisation against the illnesses that drive children into malnutrition. Implication 1 is the outlier: the passage never mentions the Public Distribution System, and who monitors it is an administrative question the text gives no basis for, which rules out A and C. D is too narrow, arbitrarily dropping maternal health and sanitation while keeping vaccination, which is no closer to the passage's language than they are. Marked MED because none of the four is named in the passage; the item turns on reading 'practical implications' as measures against child malnutrition.

items.value: Only inferences 2 and 3 - pulse cultivation pollutes less, and pulse straw improves soil quality
items.reasoning: Inference 3 is stated: Arhar straw is green, can be ploughed back and decomposes very fast, which is soil improvement. Inference 2 follows because paddy straw's high silica prevents decomposition, leaving farmers to burn it, whereas Arhar straw is ploughed back - less burning means less pollution. Inference 1 fails because the yield comparison in the passage is with existing pulse varieties, not with paddy, and income is never compared. Inference 4 overstates: the passage says paddy stalks cannot easily be salvaged or ploughed back, not that they have no use. Inference 5 is refuted by the passage itself - Arhar is also combine-harvested yet its straw is not burnt, so mechanisation cannot be the cause; the silica content of paddy straw is.

items.value: Only assumption 2 is valid - dam storage should not be filled to capacity before or during the monsoon
items.reasoning: Assumption 2 is the passage's own internationally accepted practice: the reservoir level should be kept below a certain mark before the monsoon sets in so there is room for the excess and water can be released in a regulated way, and the passage's complaint is precisely that authorities fill to the maximum even before the monsoon closes. Assumption 1 is only half the picture - the passage attributes the practice to irrigation as well as electricity generation, so blaming over-dependence on hydropower alone does not follow. Assumption 3 is a claim about how India rates dams' flood-control role that the passage never makes, and since there is no option pairing 2 with 3, the valid single assumption gives B.

items.value: Only inference 1 is valid - the economic role of the State needs to be rethought and redefined
items.reasoning: The passage says liberalisation was shaped by the government's own economic problems rather than by people's priorities or long-term development objectives, that this produced limitations in conception and design borne out by experience, and that the resulting problems must be resolved for growth to become meaningful development. Since liberalisation was itself a redefinition of the State's economic role and is judged to have been badly conceived, rethinking that role is a fair inference. Inference 2 goes beyond the text twice over: the four named crises are agriculture, infrastructure, industrialisation and education, only one of which is a social sector, and the passage says nothing at all about implementation quality or the sufficiency of investment. Marked MED because inference 1's specific phrasing is a step past the passage's own words, though it is the only defensible reading once 2 is rejected.

items.value: Neither assumption is valid
items.reasoning: Assumption 1 is absent from the passage, which never discusses global integration, exports or India's place in the world economy; its subject is the domestic conception of liberalisation. Assumption 2 is not merely absent but contradicted by the evidence the passage puts forward - jobless growth, persistent poverty and rising inequality have 'mounted as problems since economic liberalization began', and 'all these years later' four crises still constrain the economy, which is the passage's way of saying the promised long-run gains have not arrived. With both rejected the answer is D.

items.value: All three options are equally good - each leaves the customer paying 79.2 per cent of the marked price
items.reasoning: Every option applies the same three multipliers to the price: 0.9 for the 10 per cent discount, 0.8 for the 20 per cent discount and 1.1 for the 10 per cent service tax. Multiplication is commutative, so the order in which they are applied cannot change the result - each comes to 0.9 x 0.8 x 1.1 = 0.792 of the marked price. On an article priced 1000 all three options cost 792, so no option is better for the customer than another. The intuition that paying tax before the discounts is worse is wrong precisely because the discounts then apply to the tax as well.

The letter-to-number rule turns DEF into the three-digit string 456 and GHI into 789. Each given value is exactly twice that string: 456 x 2 = 912 and 789 x 2 = 1578. Applying the same rule, ABC becomes 123, and 123 x 2 = 246. Option A, 492, is what you get from doubling each digit separately, and option C, 262, fits neither pattern.

items.value: NPJM
items.reasoning: Comparing ACPQ with BESU position by position gives shifts of +1 (A to B), +2 (C to E), +3 (P to S) and +4 (Q to U). Applying the same 1, 2, 3, 4 pattern to MNGI gives M+1 = N, N+2 = P, G+3 = J and I+4 = M, that is NPJM. The distractors each break one step: NPJL takes I forward only 3, NOJM takes N forward only 1, and NPIL is wrong in the last two places.

items.value: (1/3) to the power -4, which equals 81
items.reasoning: A negative exponent on a reciprocal simply inverts it, so the four values are 2 to the 6th = 64, 4 cubed = 64, 3 to the 4th = 81 and 6 squared = 36. The largest is 81, option C. Worth noting that options A and B are equal in value at 64 despite being written differently, so neither can be the unique largest in any case.
